doc.title: Jim Hall — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Lead Belly, Charlie Christian, Lunceford, Argentina

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the blues is, and why every jazz player needs it

blocks.x: Yep. You dedicated a Bluesography…
Oh, yeah.
… to Charlie Christian and Lead Belly.
Oh, wow. Huh.
I don’t know what role they ever played in your listening history.
Oh, well, we have to talk about…
Well, (overlapping/inaudible)…
Yeah, yeah.
But Lead Belly is a surprise to me.

Yeah. Well, I must have heard him and I was really impressed by his approach to, first of all, to guitar playing and… That’s why I like… oh, what’s the guy that has a restaurant uptown I love? Blues player.
B.B. King.

B.B., yeah. I love his playing. I’d rather hear him play just maybe one or two notes than most guys play all night, ‘cause it means something. And then, and he’ll play and he can’t sort of play the guitar and sing at the same time or something. So then he’ll stop and… (laughs) But yeah, so that was… Obviously, that’s what Lead Belly… And then, I guess the Charlie Christian thing had to do with my habit. He was my spiritual awakening, (laughs) as I said, so…
You’ve got a tune dedicated to Lunceford.
Oh, wow. Yeah.
And a Canto Nostalgico.
Oh, yeah. Nostalgic song, I guess.
That you dedicated to your friends in Argentina.
Oh, yeah.
So of your worldwide…
Yeah. Yeah. I told you… was it yesterday… about having been in Argentina and having discovered all this (laughs) pretty good music that tango players are doing.
